title: Chunking strategies
summary: Split long documents into retrievable pieces that fit a model's context and return clean, relevant answers in a RAG pipeline.
objectives: Explain why chunking is needed for retrieval and long documents
Compare fixed-size, recursive, and semantic chunking strategies
Choose a sensible chunk size and overlap for a use case
Implement character and token-based chunking in Python
Preserve structure and attach metadata to each chunk
Evaluate chunking quality by inspecting retrieved results

quiz.q: Why do we chunk documents before putting them in a retrieval system?
options: To fit context limits and improve retrieval relevance
quiz.why: Chunks keep each retrieved piece focused and small enough to fit the context window, so search returns relevant passages instead of whole documents.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of chunk overlap?
options: To avoid cutting a key idea exactly at a boundary
quiz.why: Overlap repeats a little text between neighbouring chunks so a sentence or idea split across a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk.

quiz.q: Which strategy splits on natural separators like paragraphs, then sentences, falling back to characters only if needed?
quiz.why: Recursive chunking tries a priority list of separators (paragraph, line, sentence, word) so splits land on natural boundaries before resorting to raw character cuts.

quiz.q: True or false: chunk size should always be measured in characters, never tokens.
quiz.why: False. Because models bill and limit by tokens, sizing chunks in tokens is often more reliable; characters are a convenient approximation only.

quiz.q: Name one useful piece of metadata to store alongside each chunk and say why.
quiz.answer: The source document name or page number, so retrieved answers can cite where they came from.
quiz.why: Metadata such as source, title, page, or section lets you trace, filter, and cite chunks, which is essential for trustworthy RAG answers.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is a reasonable default starting point for chunk size and overlap?
quiz.answer: Around 500 to 1000 tokens per chunk with roughly 10 to 20 percent overlap, then tune by inspecting results.
quiz.why: These defaults balance enough context per chunk against retrieval precision; you adjust based on document type and observed answer quality.

body_markdown:
## Why chunking?

A language model can only read so much text at once, and a retrieval system works best when each stored piece is small and focused. **Chunking** is the act of splitting a long document into smaller pieces, called **chunks**, before you embed and store them.

If you store an entire 50-page PDF as one item, a search for one fact returns all 50 pages, most of it irrelevant. If you split it into paragraph-sized chunks, search returns just the passages that matter. Good chunking is often the single biggest lever on the quality of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system.

## The trade-off: size vs precision

Chunk size is a balance. **Large chunks** carry more surrounding context but dilute relevance and may overflow limits. **Small chunks** are precise but can lose the context needed to answer.

A common starting point is roughly **500 to 1000 tokens** per chunk. Size in **tokens**, not characters, because models limit and bill by tokens. A rough rule of thumb is one token per four characters of English, but count properly when it matters.

## Overlap

If you cut strictly every N tokens, you will sometimes slice a sentence or idea in half. **Overlap** repeats a small slice of text between neighbouring chunks so the idea survives in at least one chunk. A typical overlap is 10 to 20 percent of the chunk size.

```python
def chunk_text(text, size=800, overlap=100):
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + size
        chunks.append(text[start:end])
        start = end - overlap   # step back to create overlap
    return chunks

doc = open("report.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
print(len(chunk_text(doc)))
```

This is **fixed-size** chunking: simple and fast, but blind to structure.

## Smarter strategies

**Recursive chunking** splits on a priority list of separators — paragraphs first, then lines, then sentences, then words — so cuts land on natural boundaries. **Semantic chunking** groups sentences by meaning, keeping related ideas together. Recursive is the practical default for most text.

```python
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=800,
    chunk_overlap=100,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""],
)
chunks = splitter.split_text(doc)
print(len(chunks), "chunks")
```

## Metadata matters

Each chunk should travel with **metadata**: the source file, a title, a page or section number. This lets you cite where an answer came from and filter retrieval. Without it, a correct answer is hard to trust.

## Sizing by tokens with Claude

When the downstream model is Claude, count tokens with the Anthropic SDK so chunks fit your budget exactly. Keep your A P I key in the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
for i, ch in enumerate(chunks):
    n = client.messages.count_tokens(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ch}],
    ).input_tokens
    print(f"chunk {i}: {n} tokens")
```

## Your task

Take a long text file, chunk it three ways — fixed-size, recursive, and recursive with metadata — and inspect the boundaries of the first few chunks for each.

slides.title: Chunking strategies
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Three, where we build real applications on top of large language models. In this lesson we tackle chunking: how to split long documents into smaller pieces so a retrieval system can find the right passage and feed it to the model. Get chunking right and your whole pipeline gets better. Let's dig in.

slides.title: Why chunk at all?
bullets: Models read only a limited amount at once.
Search works best on small, focused pieces.
One huge document returns mostly noise.
slides.narration: So why chunk at all? A language model can only read so much text in one go, and a retrieval system works best when each stored piece is small and focused. If you store a fifty page document as a single item, a search for one fact hands back all fifty pages, almost all of it irrelevant. Chunking lets search return just the passages that matter.

slides.title: What is a chunk?
bullets: A chunk is one small slice of a document.
We embed and store chunks, then retrieve them.
Used in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG.
slides.narration: A chunk is simply one small slice of a document. We split the document into chunks, turn each into an embedding, and store them. Later, when a user asks a question, we retrieve the most relevant chunks and pass them to the model. This whole pattern is called Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, and chunking is its foundation.

slides.title: Size vs precision
bullets: Large chunks: more context, less precise.
Small chunks: precise, but may lose context.
Good start: 500 to 1000 tokens.
Size by tokens, not characters.
slides.narration: Chunk size is a balancing act. Large chunks carry more surrounding context but dilute relevance and may overflow limits. Small chunks are precise but can lose the context needed to answer. A good starting point is roughly five hundred to a thousand tokens. And size in tokens, not characters, because models limit and bill by tokens.

slides.title: Overlap keeps ideas whole
bullets: Cutting every N tokens can split a sentence.
Overlap repeats a little text between chunks.
Typical overlap: 10 to 20 percent.
slides.narration: If you cut strictly every N tokens, you will sometimes slice a sentence clean in half. Overlap fixes this: it repeats a small slice of text between neighbouring chunks, so an idea split across a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk. A typical overlap is ten to twenty percent of the chunk size. Notice in the code how we step back by the overlap each loop.

slides.title: Fixed-size chunking
bullets: Just cut every N characters or tokens.
Simple and fast to implement.
Blind to paragraphs and sentences.
slides.narration: The simplest approach is fixed-size chunking: just cut the text every N characters or tokens. It is fast and easy, and a fine baseline. The downside is that it is completely blind to structure. It will happily cut in the middle of a paragraph, a sentence, or even a word, which is exactly where overlap and smarter strategies earn their keep.

slides.title: Recursive chunking
bullets: Split on paragraphs, then lines, then sentences.
Falls back to characters only if needed.
The practical default for most text.
slides.code:
from langchain_text_splitters import \
    RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=800, chunk_overlap=100,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""])
chunks = splitter.split_text(doc)
slides.narration: Recursive chunking is smarter. It tries a priority list of separators: paragraphs first, then lines, then sentences, then words, falling back to raw characters only as a last resort. This means splits land on natural boundaries. For most text this is the practical default, and tools like LangChain give it to you out of the box, as shown here.

slides.title: Semantic chunking
bullets: Groups sentences by meaning, not length.
Keeps related ideas together.
More work; useful for messy documents.
slides.narration: Semantic chunking goes one step further. Instead of splitting by length, it groups sentences by meaning, so closely related ideas stay together in the same chunk. It costs more to compute and set up, but it can really help with messy or loosely structured documents. Start with recursive, and reach for semantic when retrieval quality demands it.

slides.title: Attach metadata
bullets: Store source, title, page, section.
Lets you cite where answers came from.
Enables filtering during retrieval.
slides.narration: Every chunk should travel with metadata: the source file, a title, a page number, a section. This is what lets you cite where an answer came from and filter your retrieval. Without metadata, even a correct answer is hard to trust, because you cannot show the user where it came from. Treat metadata as part of the chunk, not an afterthought.

slides.narration: Let's recap. We chunk documents to fit context limits and to make retrieval sharp and relevant. Pick a sensible size and overlap, and size by tokens when you can. Recursive chunking is your practical default, and always attach metadata so answers can be cited.
